title: Deterministic Ceiling in a Paired Evaluation of Verifier‑Augmented and LLM‑Only NetOps Agents
abstract: We conducted a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1. The design used gpt‑5‑mini as generator, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer, N=400 paired tasks (800 episodes), and shared_initial_generation semantics (one shared LLM candidate per task delivered to both conditions). Confirmatory outcomes are exact and deterministic: complete_pairs = 400; baseline_success_count = 400/400; guarded_success_count = 400/400; paired contingency n_11 = 400, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0; observed paired difference = 0.0; preregistered permutation p = 1.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). Diagnostics using execution and reconciliation artifacts show that preregistered shared_initial_generation together with reuse of the same deterministic validator created a deterministic ceiling that made the primary estimand uninformative in this run. We present the preregistered methodology, exact artifact‑grounded results, an operational diagnosis of the ceiling mechanism supported by provider and validator traces, and concrete artifact‑grounded recommendations to harden future benchmarks so they expose generator×guard interactions.

sections.introduction:
Agentic LLMs are being proposed to translate operator intent into network configuration artifacts and to drive staged change workflows (canaries, progressive rollout, rollback). Prior studies establish that LLMs can produce syntactically plausible configuration templates in controlled corpora and emulated testbeds, and separate work shows that verifier‑guided generate–validate–repair loops can reduce syntactic and semantic errors in infrastructure‑as‑code. The central operational safety question motivating this study is end‑to‑end: how do generator variability, runtime verification, staged rollout semantics, repair, and rollback interact to determine safe‑deploy outcomes in NetOps pipelines?

This paper reports a preregistered paired evaluation under ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1 asking whether integrating a deterministic runtime validator with an LLM generator increases paired safe‑deploy rate relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. The primary estimand was the paired difference in safe‑deploy rate (guarded − baseline) measured on N=400 preregistered paired tasks using a paired‑binary confirmatory design. We executed the registered protocol, archived every runtime and analysis artifact, and here report the exact confirmatory outputs together with an evidence‑grounded diagnosis of why the design produced a deterministic ceiling and concrete, actionable hardening recommendations.
sections.related_work: This study sits at the intersection of three literatures. First, intent→configuration generation: recent prototypes and datasets show feasibility of mapping natural language intent to device configuration, but evaluations are often limited to curated corpora or emulated topologies and generalization gaps remain. Representative examples include intent‑to‑configuration systems and pretrained/fine‑tuning approaches that demonstrate template generation but highlight dataset and scope limits. Second, verifier‑guided workflows and deterministic verification: work in IaC (verifier‑guided training and verification in TerraFormer and related systems) and deterministic network verifiers demonstrate that strong verifiers catch many classes of offline errors; however, explicit closed‑loop runtime integration and empirical studies of generator×verifier dynamics in staged rollout settings are limited. Third, agentic and tool‑augmented LLM architectures (ReAct, RAG, multi‑agent orchestrations) broaden AIOps capabilities but introduce new failure modes—hallucination, tool misuse, overconfident outputs—that motivate runtime guardrails and staged deployments. Survey and evaluation‑gap reviews call for action‑aware benchmarks that combine generation, runtime blocking, staged rollout, repair, rollback, and provenance; our benchmark implements a compact variant of these desiderata and, importantly, reveals a concrete statistical pitfall for paired designs when generation and scoring variance are conflated.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimands. The study preregistration specified a paired binary confirmatory design with exactly N=400 paired tasks and primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The preregistered primary test was a permutation‑based paired difference test; an exact McNemar two‑sided test and paired bootstrap CIs were prespecified for corroboration. Secondary prespecified outcomes included bootstrap CIs for median time‑to‑rollback and counts of repair attempts.

Execution contract and critical design choices. Execution used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter with declared generator gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 used both as runtime guard and as the post‑hoc scorer. The preregistration set shared_initial_generation = true (independent_condition_generation = false): for each task a single LLM candidate was generated and that identical candidate was delivered to both baseline and guarded episodes. This choice intentionally isolated the validator’s acceptance decision on identical generator outputs and limited model‑call budget (model_calls_used = 400 for 800 episodes). The adapter permitted up to one repair call in the guarded episode; repair_applied was recorded and, empirically, repair_applied = false across episodes.

Task generation, replay, and scoring. Tasks were generated deterministically by a seed‑controlled task generator that produced per‑task difficulty metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, pattern, required_command_count, level ∈ {medium, hard, very_hard}). Deterministic replay checks were applied and passed for all pairs. Scoring and runtime blocking used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 performing full intent‑constraint validation; validator traces record validation_before/after, final_configuration, repair_applied, and validity decisions. All design choices, seeds, executions, and analysis procedures were preregistered and all runtime and analysis artifacts were archived without manual adjudication.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and reproducibility checks. The run started 2026‑08‑29T18:23:37Z and completed 2026‑08‑29T19:12:38Z. Planned episodes = 800; completed episodes = 800; failed episodes = 0; model_calls_used = 400 (shared initial generation). Deterministic replay checks passed for all pairs; no exclusions were recorded.

Confirmatory outcomes (artifact‑grounded). The archived confirmatory analysis reports complete_pairs = 400; baseline_success_count = 400 (baseline_success_rate = 1.0); guarded_success_count = 400 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n_11 = 400 with n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0, yielding observed paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. The preregistered permutation test returned p = 1.0 and the exact McNemar two‑sided test returned p = 1.0. The paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). Cohen’s h = 0.0. These numeric values are reproduced directly from the archived analysis outputs and are exact under the deterministic execution contract.

Repair, rollback, difficulty aggregation, and provider diagnostics. Across all 800 episodes repair_applied = false and no rollbacks were invoked; validator traces indicate validation_after.final_state matched expected_final_state for accepted configurations. The archived task manifest yields the following difficulty distribution extracted verbatim: medium: 80 tasks (20.0%); hard: 160 tasks (40.0%); very_hard: 160 tasks (40.0%). Provider and reconciliation diagnostics record hosted_model_call_event_count = 400, cache_miss_count = 400, stage_counts indicating shared_initial_generation = 400, and condition_counts indicating shared = 400. These diagnostics empirically document the shared generation semantics and an absence of cross‑condition model‑call variation.
sections.discussion:
Operational diagnosis: deterministic ceiling mechanism. Two preregistered choices together forced the observed ceiling. First, shared_initial_generation removed generator variance by delivering identical LLM outputs to baseline and guarded episodes. Second, the runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer were the same deterministic implementation. When the deterministic validator accepts the shared candidate at runtime, both conditions necessarily record safe‑deploy outcomes and the paired difference is forced to zero. This is a construct‑validity outcome of the frozen design: the protocol measured validator acceptance on identical candidates rather than the effect of introducing an independent runtime guard into an otherwise independent generator process.

Statistical and inferential implications. The confirmatory tests correctly report p = 1.0 and the paired bootstrap CI correctly collapses to a point mass at zero; these are mathematically appropriate given the data. However, these inferential outputs convey no information about generator×guard closed‑loop dynamics because the design prevented the guard from having an opportunity to intervene. The preregistered power rationale assumed non‑ceiling baseline failure rates; that assumption was falsified by the frozen generator+validator pairing and thus the original power justification does not apply to this run.

Hardening recommendations grounded in archived artifacts. To preserve opportunities for runtime guards to accept, block, or request repair, future preregistered designs should avoid conflating generator variance with scorer invariance. Concrete, implementable recommendations supported by the archived manifests and traces are:
1) Independent per‑condition generation (independent_condition_generation = true) so each condition draws its own LLM candidate and generator variance is preserved; this directly enables generator×guard interactions to manifest. 
2) Use a distinct post‑hoc scorer or held‑out adjudicator (different implementation or a validator with stochastic perturbation) so runtime blocking is not numerically identical to measurement. 
3) Controlled adversarial seeding to guarantee nontrivial baseline failure rates (select or seed tasks that the generator is likely to fail without verifier intervention). 
4) Difficulty‑stratified sampling to ensure sufficient representation of very_hard tasks; the archived manifest already contains per‑task difficulty labels enabling deterministic stratified resampling. 
5) Record instrumented mitigation metrics (repair_attempts, repairs_applied, time‑to‑rollback) as explicit numeric outcomes so the benchmark captures intermediate mitigation activity even when final accept rates are high. 
Each recommendation can be implemented deterministically using artifacts already in the archive (task manifest difficulty labels, validator traces containing repair_applied and validation timestamps, and provider audit logs showing generation semantics).

Broader implications. The observed ceiling is an instructive failure mode for benchmark design: paired designs that intentionally share initial generator outputs can validly isolate scorer behavior on identical candidates, but they are unsuitable when the scientific goal is to measure closed‑loop generator×guard interactions. Researchers must align generation semantics and scoring semantics with the estimand of interest during preregistration.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline under ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1. Under the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator pairing, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and both conditions produced 100% safe‑deploy across N=400 pairs (paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0). The deterministic ceiling is a design artifact caused by identical per‑pair generation and reuse of a deterministic validator for runtime blocking and post‑hoc scoring; it renders the primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard closed‑loop interactions in this run. We archive the preregistration and full execution/analysis artifacts to enable exact reproduction of these findings. The artifact‑grounded hardening recommendations supplied here (independent generation per condition, distinct scorer, controlled adversarial seeding, difficulty stratification, and mitigation metrics) provide concrete steps to preserve statistical signal when evaluating runtime verifier utility in NetOps settings. Future runs that implement these hardening steps—possible using the archived task manifest and validator traces—can exercise blocking, repair, and rollback behaviors meaningfully and restore inferential relevance for the primary estimand.

disclosure_statement: Declared generator: gpt‑5‑mini. Orchestration: hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family with shared_initial_generation semantics (independent_condition_generation = false) as preregistered. Runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer: deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Task generator: deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Preregistration: cnsmauto‑3d2k‑prereg‑v1. The immutable initial master prompt is archived as provenance/master_prompt.txt with SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. The guarded condition routed the shared LLM candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 which deterministically accepted or blocked candidates per the preregistered adapter policy; the adapter allowed up to one repair call per task but none were applied. All runtime calls, raw outputs, validator traces, deterministic replay checks, exclusion logs, and analysis artifacts are archived in the bundled artifact set and were used without manual adjudication.
limitations: Benchmark hardness and ceiling effect: under preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 so the guard had no opportunity to alter outcomes; this makes the primary estimand effectively untestable in this run and invalidates the original power rationale.

Model and scope: the experiment used a single generator (gpt-5-mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); results do not generalize across models, validators, or production heterogeneity.

Construct validity: the same deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementation served as both runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer; this conflation produces concordant acceptance/scoring and limits inference about independent closed‑loop verifier utility.

Shared candidate semantics: preregistered shared_initial_generation (one LLM generation per task shared by both conditions) intentionally reduces generation variance and therefore limits inference to the validator’s behavior on identical candidates rather than full generator+guard closed‑loop interactions.

Synthetic environment and external validity: the simulator and validator do not fully model production telemetry noise, operator workflows, or adversarial actor behaviours; external validity to live networks is limited.

Adversarial robustness untested: adversarial or distribution‑shifted prompts and generator faults that could trigger guard interventions were not exercised in this run and remain open for future work.

Aggregated difficulty reporting: the full per‑task difficulty labels for all N=400 are archived in the task manifest and can be aggregated by auditors; Table 1 reports the artifact‑extracted aggregated counts and percentages.
